About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Mathematics and Statistics Year 11
of the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Mathematics and Statistics Year 11 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Mathematics and Statistics Year 11 is
proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum
Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Mathematics and Statistics Year 11 will be required to start using it in
Year 11 from 1 January 2028.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  skills in logical thinking, numerical fluency, and data interpretation, and             architecture, finance, education, and logistics.
  strengthens students’ foundational mathematical knowledge.



Through the study of Mathematics and Statistics, students are taught to apply
foundational mathematical knowledge and further develop number, algebra,
measurement, geometry, probability, and statistics concepts and application
expertise. They apply mathematical principles and procedures to solve problems,
interpret information, and model situations. Students use numerical, algebraic,
graphical, and geometric methods to investigate relationships, recognise patterns,
and communicate mathematical ideas using appropriate representations.

Mathematics and Statistics provides students with the knowledge and practices to
collect, analyse and interpret statistical and probabilistic data. Students develop the
ability to use disciplinary knowledge to evaluate data and communicate their
understanding in written form.

As students’ progress through Year 11 Mathematics and Statistics, they are
supported to develop their understanding of mathematical and statistical disciplinary-
specific use of symbols, notation, and terminology. This enables students to evidence
thinking and reasoning using accurate calculations, algebraic manipulation, graphical
representations, statistical analysis.

The teaching of all knowledge and practices is compulsory. Schools can determine
how learning is organised across the year, including integrating content from multiple
elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth. Examples within the
teaching sequence and contexts in brackets signified with ‘e.g.’ are provided as
guidance only; provided the intended knowledge and practices are met, schools and
teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local environments,
iwi and hapū connections, student interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to provide clarity about what
subject-specific literacy is to be taught. Disciplinary writing is organised into a
knowledge component that is consistent across all year levels and a practice
component that is sequenced across years.
